mcqs.question: Why does the feature-flag client evaluate isEnabled against a local cache instead of calling the backend on every check?
options: Because the backend only accepts one request per flag per day
Because targeting rules cannot be evaluated remotely
Because Context objects cannot be serialized over a network
So flag checks stay fast and don't introduce a new network-dependent failure mode into every call site that checks a flag
mcqs.explanation: Local, in-memory evaluation is what keeps flag checks cheap and resilient to backend slowness or outages, since a check never waits on a network round-trip. There's no such request-rate restriction, targeting rules evaluate fine locally once rules are cached, and Context objects aren't sent over the network at check time at all.

mcqs.question: In CachedFeatureFlagClient, why does a failed refresh log a warning and keep the existing cache instead of clearing it?
options: A stale-but-recent flag value is almost always a better outcome for callers than immediately falling back to every flag's hardcoded default
Clearing the cache would cause a compile error in the refresh method
The backend requires the client to always retain its most recent successful response
It has no real effect on caller behavior either way
mcqs.explanation: Keeping the last-known-good cache on a failed refresh means callers keep seeing recent, likely-correct flag values instead of an abrupt jump to every flag's fallback default. There's no compile-time restriction here, no such backend requirement, and the choice meaningfully changes what callers observe.

mcqs.question: What should isEnabled return when the backend is unreachable and the flag isn't in the cache at all yet?
options: Throw an exception so the caller is forced to handle the failure explicitly
The flag's own pre-configured default value, chosen when the flag was created based on its actual risk
Always return true, since enabling a feature is safer than disabling it
Always return false, regardless of what the flag is for
mcqs.explanation: A per-flag default lets the flag's creator decide fail-open or fail-closed based on that specific flag's risk, rather than one blanket answer for every flag. Throwing risks taking down unrelated code, and always returning true or always false ignores that different flags carry very different risk profiles.

mcqs.question: Why is it a mistake for a flag-evaluation failure to throw an exception that propagates to the calling code?
options: Exceptions thrown from isEnabled are automatically retried by the runtime
It would make the FeatureFlagClient interface impossible to implement
A feature flag check is meant to be a low-risk, incidental part of a request path, so an exception there can take down unrelated code that has nothing to do with flags
It's actually the correct behavior, since silent failures are always worse than loud ones
mcqs.explanation: Letting a flag check fail loudly turns an unrelated flag-service hiccup into an outage for whatever code happened to check a flag, a disproportionate blast radius for something this incidental. There's no automatic retry here, the interface works fine synchronous and non-throwing, and a safe default is the better choice, not a blanket 'loud is always better' rule.
